content: This document is an updated Cochrane Review, originally published in 2004 and updated in 2007, focusing on the use of antibiotic prophylaxis in clean and clean-contaminated ear surgeries. Ear surgeries are commonly performed to treat conditions such as chronic otitis media, ossicular chain disorders, tympanic membrane perforations, and otitis media with effusion. Postoperative infections in these surgeries can lead to complications, including wound infections, middle ear or mastoid infections causing ear canal discharge, failure of the tympanic membrane to heal, or labyrinthitis due to infection in or near the inner ear. These complications can result in significant patient discomfort, increased morbidity, and higher healthcare costs. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of local and/or systemic antibiotics in preventing complications such as postoperative discharge, graft failure, and labyrinthitis in patients undergoing clean or clean-contaminated ear surgeries. The review excluded skull base surgeries and included randomized or quasi-randomized trials comparing antibiotic prophylaxis (administered locally or systemically at or around the time of surgery) to placebo, no antibiotics, or alternative interventions. The outcomes assessed included infection rates, ear discharge, graft failure, labyrinthitis, and adverse effects of antibiotic prophylaxis. The search for relevant studies was comprehensive, covering multiple databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), PubMed, EMBASE, and others, with the most recent search conducted on August 31, 2009. Eleven studies met the inclusion criteria for the review. The methodological quality of these studies ranged from fair to good, but many lacked sufficient methodological detail. Despite variations in how outcomes were defined across studies, it was possible to pool the results for analysis. The findings of the review indicated no significant differences between groups receiving antibiotic prophylaxis and control groups (placebo or no antibiotics) in terms of reducing postoperative infections, graft failures, ear canal discharge, or adverse drug effects. Based on these results, the authors concluded that there is no strong evidence to support the widespread use of prophylactic antibiotics in clean and clean-contaminated ear surgeries for reducing postoperative complications such as wound infections, ear discharge, labyrinthitis, or graft failure.
